planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun for the richest gold color; this sport of California privet keeps its bright yellow leaf margins best with several hours of direct sun daily.

directions: This golden-leaved sport of California privet carries broad leaves splashed and margined in bright yellow around a green center, giving it strong ornamental impact as a color accent hedge, low screen, or contrast planting against darker evergreens. Color is brightest in full sun and fades toward chartreuse-green in shade, so site it where it gets ample direct light. It responds well to regular shearing, which also keeps the naturally vigorous plant compact and encourages fresh, brightly colored new growth throughout the season. Like the straight species it tolerates poor soil, urban pollution, and hard pruning, though gardeners near wooded natural areas should shear before flowering to limit self-seeding.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun, which is essential for developing and holding this hybrid's signature golden-yellow foliage.

directions: Golden Vicary is a naturally occurring hybrid between California privet and border privet, selected for its consistently bright golden-yellow foliage that holds color through the growing season better than most other yellow-leaved shrubs, making it one of the most cold-hardy golden hedge plants available for northern gardens. It is semi-evergreen to deciduous depending on winter severity and tolerates hard, repeated shearing into a formal hedge or can be left looser as an informal golden screen or specimen. Full sun is essential for good color; in shade the foliage turns dull green. Established plants tolerate heat, drought, and a wide range of soils, and light summer shearing after the small white flower clusters fade helps maintain a dense, tidy form and limits seed production.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; border privet is markedly more cold-hardy than the evergreen Southern privets and suits northern climates where those species fail.

directions: Border privet is a cold-hardy deciduous shrub with an attractive, gracefully arching, horizontally tiered branching habit distinct from the stiffer, more upright growth of most privets, making it useful both as a clipped hedge and as an unsheared specimen where its natural fountain-like form can be appreciated. Small white flower clusters open in late spring to early summer along the branches, followed by blue-black berries that persist into winter and are eaten by birds. It tolerates a wide range of soils, urban pollution, and both sun and considerable shade, and it withstands hard renewal pruning if a hedge becomes leggy or overgrown. Because it self-seeds and has naturalized in parts of the northeastern and midwestern United States, gardeners near wild areas should shear before flowering to reduce berry production.
sources: USDA Forest Service Fire Effects Information System

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped shrubs in spring or fall in nearly any well-drained soil in full sun for best variegation; this cultivar is slower and less seed-prolific than the plain green species.

directions: This variegated selection of glossy privet carries broad, leathery leaves irregularly marked in cream, gray-green, and pink-tinged tones around a dark green center, giving it far more year-round ornamental interest than the solid-green species while retaining the same large, upright growth habit. It can be trained as a big screening hedge with regular shearing or allowed to develop into a small multi-trunked evergreen tree where space allows, and its slower growth rate compared to the straight species makes it easier to keep in bounds. Site in full sun for the strongest variegation, since shaded plants tend to revert toward plainer green foliage. It shares the species' tolerance for heat, drought, and poor soil, and shearing before the fragrant white flower clusters open in late spring helps limit berry set and self-seeding near natural areas.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox
